factors.desc: Favorable or neutral coverage across the meta's IP archetypes and color strategies. With an expanded 15-deck meta field, decks with fewer polarized matchups perform more reliably across tournament swiss rounds.
Efficient AP usage and energy curve optimization for early and mid-game board development. Includes the ability to deploy threats ahead of curve and maintain proactive pressure.
Maximum damage output potential through Impact, Double Attack, Damage 2, and high BP thresholds. Measures how decisively a deck can close games once its win condition is assembled.
Overall value and composition of triggers in the deck's life area, including Color triggers for resource generation, Active triggers for board impact, and Final triggers for last-resort defense.
Reliable access to key characters and combo pieces through draw, search, and filtering effects. Decks that consistently assemble their core strategy outperform those reliant on natural draws.
Energy and AP economy, hand size management, and long-term card advantage. Measures how efficiently a deck converts its resources into board presence and damage over the course of a game.
Decision tree depth, AP sequencing complexity, and the gap between average and optimal play lines. Decks that reward mastery with significantly higher win rates score well here.
Ability to recover from life damage pressure, board wipes, and resource deficit through trigger activations, defensive keywords, and comeback mechanics.
Adaptable game plans, multi-color tech options, and the ability to pivot between aggressive and defensive postures depending on game state and matchup.

Ability to interfere with the opponent's board state, hand, or game plan through removal, Snipe, retire effects, and denial of key setups. Increasingly relevant as combo-oriented IPs populate the meta.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena, this aggro-tempo Saito list is fairly straightforward: it fills the energy line quickly with four-copy cheap characters and then pushes damage, so most turns have a clear main line. Its difficulty comes from deciding when to commit Gatotsu or Evil-Immediate-Slaughter bursts and from managing a hand that can stall without draw, while its weak triggers and matchup-dependent race against faster Sakamoto Days and REZ lists keep errors costly.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Asuka's Aggro-Tempo shell plays a straightforward curve of cheap Rei and Mari bodies into mid-cost threats, so most turns offer one clear play and the pilot's main job is attacking efficiently and managing when to commit. Matchup choices matter against faster aggro or slow fringe decks, and misplayed attacks or overextension can cost games against a stronger Evangelion Raid build, but the deck's cards do most of the work when drawn well.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Eva is a fairly straightforward midrange-tempo shell: mono-color energy rarely blocks a play, the 1/2/3 AP ramp is predictable, and the front-line Mari bodies trade on BP with little sequencing subtlety, so the obvious line usually wins. Its difficulty rises in matchup handling against fast Sakamoto Days and REZ aggro lists and in judging when to race versus stabilize, while limited finishers and disruption mean a misjudged race is hard to recover from.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Sakamoto Store is a low-cost aggro-tempo deck whose core plan is to deploy cheap Taro and Hana bodies early and push damage with Shin Asakura, so most turns have one or two obvious plays and the average turn carries only moderate branching. Its main difficulty comes from the seven Taro numbers diluting the curve, which forces choices about which copy to play and when to hold back, and from being unable to clear big blockers, which requires reading when to commit into a stall. Because the cards themselves deliver a fast board, a new pilot keeps much of the deck's win rate, but close games are decided by correct attack sequencing and matchup-specific pressure decisions.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Shin Asakura Aggro-Tempo is a fairly straightforward curve deck: most turns are about developing the energy line and attacking with four-copy staples, so decisions per turn are moderate rather than dense. Sequencing matters mainly around AP and energy spend and when to commit attackers, and misplays are often recoverable given the deck's tempo, though stalling against blockers punishes poor pacing. The cards do much of the work on a good draw, which is why autopilot is high relative to peers.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, Solo Leveling Purple is a midrange deck whose Shadow Soldiers energy line and Raid payoffs produce several real per-turn choices about what to deploy, hold, and attack with, though many turns still follow a clear script. Its skill demand rises on matchups: the slow opening must be played around against Aggro-Tempo decks, and the Raid chain is fragile to removal, so pilots must read each opponent's role and protect Shadow Soldiers. The deck's consistent core assembly and raw power soften the penalty for minor misplays, leaving the autopilot factor near the middle of the range.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Raid tempo requires choosing which active character to Raid into, when to commit AP and energy in the Main Phase, and when to attack, so most turns carry several real decisions. Sequencing the energy line before the Raid targets matters, and the 1-AP opening makes early misplays costly, but the deck's core lines are fairly direct. Matchup adjustments against slower midrange boards versus faster aggro are meaningful but not deck-redefining.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard's tournament field, Evangelion Ragu asks for a dense, fast curve whose energy-line and AP sequencing rewards careful turn planning, especially the ordering of AP-card switching against the energy line build. Its skill ceiling is the highest among tempo decks, so decisions about when to push Raid and when to hold back are frequent, but the core Rei and Proto Type-00 plays are fairly obvious, which keeps autopilot high. Errors in the early build turns are costly against racing aggro, though the deck's own cards carry much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Heisuke Mashimo aggro-tempo is a low, dense curve that mostly plays out the same way, so most turns offer one obvious deployment and attack, placing it below the typical competitive deck in decision density. Sequencing matters in choosing between Heisuke, Shin and Taro versions and in when to commit to the energy line, and the matchup shifts how many characters to push versus hold back against stable blockers, which keeps those components near the middle. Four-of key characters make the deck very predictable, so it wins largely on its cards and forgives many misplays, though a misjudged race against fast aggro decks can still be punished.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Sakamoto Days Aggro-Tempo asks the pilot to choose which characters to play and in what order to reach the energy line, with several real decisions per turn across the Start, Movement, Main, and Attack Phases. Its multi-character curve and the need to commit AP and energy correctly make sequencing matter, but the core plan of developing early and attacking is fairly straightforward, so it sits near the middle of the competitive range for Union Arena Standard. The deck has a high power ceiling and a strong default line, so a fair share of its results come from the cards themselves, though thin draw and little removal mean misplays on the curve are costly.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Tokyo Ghoul Ayato/Juzo is a midrange shell with a few meaningful decisions per turn around deploying characters and timing raid chains, which sits near the middle of the competitive Union Arena field. Sequencing matters for raid and BP trades but is mostly visible rather than hidden in response windows, and the Ayato playset gives a consistent early line that carries much of the win rate. Its data is inconsistent (foreign-IP cards in the list), so these scores are lower-confidence estimates.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena decks, the Kenshin Himura Raid Midrange list asks for steady per-turn choices about which Kenshin number to deploy, when to Raid, and how to split energy and AP, so decision density and matchup adjustment run above the median. Sequencing across the Start-to-End phases and the choice of when to switch AP cards to resting matter in key turns, while the reliable Himura core and cheap energy bodies let a new pilot still win a fair share of games, keeping autopilot moderate-to-low.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Eren/Zeke Rumbling midrange deck asks for real per-turn choices: when to commit AP and energy toward Rumbling and Doomsday Titan, which characters to raid with, and when to hold back against aggro. Sequencing matters around the energy line and AP ramp, but the deck does not depend on tight response-window timing. Its slow opening and reliance on a late-game top end make misplays costly, while its power ceiling means a clean draw can win without precise play, keeping autopilot moderate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Among competitive Union Arena Standard decks this is a midrange Zeke Jaeger deck that asks for real turn-by-turn choices about when to commit energy-line bodies and when to switch Zeke versions to the front line, but its core plan is fairly direct. Sequencing matters mostly in getting the energy line up for turns 2-3, so timing sensitivity is moderate. The plan shifts against fast pressure like Sakamoto Days and REZ - Rem, so matchup variance is above average, while the playset-heavy build and large bodies let a straightforward pilot win many games, keeping autopilot high.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: A Tempo deck built around cheap Proto Type-00 turn-one and turn-two plays and a Rei Ayanami Raid line gives the pilot a moderate number of real choices per turn, mainly sequencing the energy line and deciding when to commit Raid targets. Its single-plan shell and lack of finishers keep matchup variance and the autopilot factor near the middle, while racing aggro decks punish a stalled opening hand, so errors cost noticeably. Overall it rates as a mid-difficulty tournament deck relative to other Standard Union Arena lists.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Kagurabachi is an aggro-tempo deck whose main job is to build a reliable early curve of cheap characters on the energy line and then spend AP each turn on the obvious plays, so most turns carry only a few real choices (what to deploy, when to attack) rather than long branching sequences. Sequencing is mostly straightforward, but the deck has a notable race dynamic: stalling on early characters or flooding can cost the game, and being out-curved by faster lists punishes poor pacing choices. Overall it is moderately demanding, easier to pilot in the early turns than the more complex decks of the format, with its skill expression concentrated in tempo management and matchup-based racing.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

Matchup adjustments are real because the deck is slow against aggro, yet the core plan of building the energy line with Grave and Cinderella stays fairly consistent. Its reliable playsets make the obvious line win a fair share of games, while mulligan and energy-line stalls in awkward hands punish misjudgment moderately.

skillRating.label: Intermediate

Its reliance on four-copy core cards and a consistent mid-curve keeps the autopilot factor moderate, and the plan changes only modestly by matchup, so its difficulty sits mid-range among competitive Union Arena decks.

skillRating.label: Intermediate

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly

skillRating.label: Intermediate

It needs a strong draw to function, so it is less autopiloted than a power-heavy deck, and it loses to fast pressure decks, which makes its matchup demands noticeable.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Hakuri Sazanami Midrange is a straightforward board-building deck: its plan is to deploy bodies, reach the energy line and trade on BP, so it offers modest per-turn choices and light sequencing demands. Its cards do much of the work, so a new pilot retains much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
